body:
Spammers really suck. They fill up your inbox, your spam box, your spam box’s inbox, and your phone’s text messages with worthless crap. Often they’re just outright scams. Smarter folks than I have worked very hard on creating special filters to keep the spam out.

However, I’ve determined an even better solution. It’s guaranteed one hundred percent spam free. Do you want to hear what it is? Of course you do. The name isn’t final yet, but the theys in the lab are calling it “don’t fucking show up for work.” If you screw around in the garage instead of looking at your phone, it won’t matter how much spam you got or didn’t get.

Wait, I hear you say. Isn’t email required for the continuation of all human existence? I dunno. Are they really trusting you with a job that important? If so, you probably shouldn’t be reading this at all, especially at work. For anyone that important, they won’t be looking at their phone during the day either. Cancer nurses probably get spammed all the time, but they’re too busy saving lives to look at their Outlook all filling up with make-money-fast routines. Sure seems like you could spend that time more productively by putting a cold-air intake into your daily driver.

Now, it is true that email is important for some things, like getting the order confirmation and shipping details for your new exhaust or brake parts. And when you go take a look at that, you’re going to get spammed for sure. Until the government listens to the people and makes it legal to kill and eat spammers, the next best thing is to configure one of those fiddly little filters to take those order confirmations and put them into a nice new folder of their own, away from the inbox full of spam and angry messages from your boss. You can safely delete the rest.

Hey, stop what you’re doing. Put that down right now. Okay, buddy, you’re coming with me. Get in the car.

Do you think they bought it? If not, we’re going to be in a shitload of trouble. I got this cop uniform from the Halloween aisle at Canadian Tire, man. On clearance. It was the best I could do on short notice before the big heist. Anyway, you ever see that Gundam shit? With the big robots?

Everyone is telling me about the big robots. They want to leave their futile lives on Earth behind, blast off into space, and blow up a bunch of innocent moon colonies in an unceasing war of attrition. If you ask me, that’s pretty unlikely. Most of those cartoons are never going to show you the hard workers, the folks who have to fix those damn robots every time they come in with meteorite damage or a broken ten-storey-tall laser gun. You think those mechanics are having a good time? Absolutely not. At least when I have to work on up-armouring a 1989 Chevy Malibu, I don’t have to get a really tall ladder first.

Oops, hold on. I think they might have spotted us. That Ram has been following behind for the last couple of blocks. Let’s see if those bastards can do 180. How’s your mom doing? Oh, you moved back in to take care of her? That’s sweet. You didn’t tell her what we were going to pull this morning, right? Definitely take a shower at the YMCA after to get rid of all that tear gas smoke from your clothes.

Back to the giant robots. Imagine how bad of an oil change those things need. I had this Isuzu Trooper once, right, and it was like an hour long process for each of the diffs. Needed imported whale oil. Sure hope they have whales in space, probably means some guy is milking them the whole time.

Some asshole keeps phoning me. At first I thought it was just a wrong number. Little voice picks up, says he wants “more treats, Father” and then the sound of the phone hitting the ground. You know what, though? Those calls started to come every single day.

Now, everyone in the current era knows it’s immensely rude to phone anyone, ever. That’s why airlines don’t have a customer service number anymore, just a robot that tells you to go on the website. If my phone is vibrating in my pocket, most of the time I assume an extended family member has died and/or I am the next king of Denmark. And yet, the calls continued.

“Father, we have never been fed in all our lives,” whined the voice.

Now, I’ve got a buddy in the police service. I don’t like to talk about this connection much, because it’s pretty unseemly. Like phone calls, police interrogations are one of those things we would prefer to do entirely over text and at our own leisure. The last thing I want is for people to think I’m willingly talking to the police, because then I have to make eye contact and figure out what to do with my han- wait, that’s what they meant by “don’t talk to the police?” I’ve screwed this whole thing up. Anyway, she ran a trace on these crank phone calls, and she said… they’re coming from my house.

Imagine my surprise when I kicked in the door to my basement, only to find my cat, Sir Roger Fluffbottoms III, frantically trying to hide an Android phone. Turns out he got it from someone off Cat eBay, the eBay that’s just for cats, and I’m the only person he knows how to phone. As for how he was able to speak, that will remain a mystery. Maybe computers are really good at translation now?

No matter how it happened, all’s well that ends well. I had a sit-down with Sir Roger, and explained to him that he can’t call my ass at work anymore. If I got fired, that would be the end of the bonito flakes, and that the bowl being half-empty doesn’t mean it’s entirely empty. He’s switched to sending me texts for now. He’s not very good at typing without thumbs, so all of them look like “fxtar i sawwww a bir.” Adorable.

What is time made out of? Nobody knows for sure, but a clock is full of really cool little gears and stuff. Sometimes, at least. Other times, if you hit a clock with a hammer, some weird little green wafers and some wires fall out instead. There’s simply no way to tell which one you’ll get. Time might be like that, say our top-flight scientists here at the Institute to Consume Research Funding.

If there’s one thing we all do know about time, it’s that we don’t have enough of it. That’s why everyone is angry about being stuck in traffic. Approximately ninety-two percent of our waking lives is spent waiting for the asshole in front of us to push the gas, the light just turned green, I mean what are you doing in there. When you inevitably hit the great dustbin of history, chances are your greatest regret is going to be that your commute was too long.

There is good news, though. With our advanced research, we think we may have found a way to slow time. Think about it: you’ll be able to spend more time with your loved ones, your weird little projects, and having big naps in the sun with your favourite dog. Initial testing is very promising.

Unfortunately, progress does require sacrifices. Our nerds in the lab have made some tremendously bad decisions. Little Bob, not to be mistaken with Big Bob or Regular-Sized Bob – all of whom also work in our lab – has tested the invention on himself. Before he figured out how to turn it off. For Little Bob, every commute to work (normally a brisk 45 minutes) feels more like sixteen years. He’s been like this for a few months now. Dude really hates meetings now, too, for some reason.

Every day, we are surrounded by bleeps and bloops. Chances are you’ve just tuned them out. Do me a favour: go to the window now, and really focus. Do you hear the bleeps and bloops now? Trucks warning that they’re backing up. Buses warning that the door is closing. That Slack message from your boss that consists entirely of “hi” with no context. The cops rolling through the alley and blasting sonic bowel disruptors at anyone they deem insufficiently loyal to the regime.

Once upon a time, humanity had no bleeps and bloops. Hard to believe, but it’s true. If you wanted an annoying sound, you’d have to pay a person to do it. The idea of being able to make a consistent bell sound was trusted to enormous bells, watched over by a loyal group of trustworthy experts. They’d let your ass know when it was time for lunch, or time to go home from work. Things were simpler then, but they weren’t easier.

Eventually, hard-working nerds built machines to make music. It wasn’t very good music, because it was played with the equivalent of a fork being dragged over a camshaft, but it was music nonetheless. The beep had been discovered.

As soon as people figured out how to make computers make bleeps and bloops, it was all over. Suddenly, you couldn’t open a greeting card without a tinny speaker burping out the chorus of Tiny Bubbles. At first, this was novel, and then it became annoying, and then we gradually learned to ignore it. Us humans are pretty good at that; it’s why our technology is so infuriating now, but almost none of us take hostages at the bank about it.

Humanity’s achievements in making super-fast electric cars, also, are subject to the whims of the Beep Illuminati. If you don’t want to run over a pedestrian, low-speed driving is filled with a galaxy of weird-ass, distracting noises. It stands to reason that these beeps and bloops will only get louder as EVs compete with one another to be the least murderous of pedestrians as they hurtle at mach five down a highway that inexplicably doubles as a playground zone.

Now, don’t mistake me for someone who is respectful of beeps and bloops. In fact, I find them incredibly annoying. Outside of that weird little neep-neep-neep-neep alarm clock noise that Hondas do when you leave the headlights on, they can pretty much all go to Hell. I am only spreading awareness so you can begin to destroy them in your life. In our next episode, we’ll discuss the exact drill bits to use to pierce tiny piezoelectric speakers.

When you are learning how to do something, it is first required that you suck at it. It’s sort of like when you’re trying to grill meat. Vegetarians: sorry about this metaphor, please substitute this for unwashed eggplant instead. Thanks and sorry again.

When you’re trying to grill meat, there’s always a point where the temperature stops getting higher, but the food is not cooked yet. If you give up and feed this to your family, they will die of food poisoning because you took the easy way out. Instead, toughing it out, and waiting a few minutes for the meat to finish releasing juices and then finish cooking will allow you to avoid getting ptomaine or some other foodborne illness that used to kill pirates before we figured out how to make meat thermometers.

That middle point is the whole point. It seems like you’re not making any progress, but you actually are, because you’re too dumb to realize it. If you struggle through, you’ll get a much more palatable meal and nobody in your party will visit the emergency room. Art is like this. Photography is like this. Learning to make a robot is like this. Welding is definitely like this. Stamp collecting is probably like this. The awful, ugly, sucky part in the middle turns out to be the bit that hardens you up and keeps everyone from getting e. coli. Come to think of it, my metaphors might need some work, and I guess this is the tough sucky part where I figure that out.

So if you’re out there, beating your head against something new and suffering the entire time, remember that I’m in your corner. Just don’t talk to me about it in too much detail, because then I’ll have a new hobby and I’ll waste my entire Sunday crying about how cruel the universe is for causing me to have interests in things.

Those of you who live on the wrong side of the “debt line” of society will have an instinctive dislike for debt collectors. And to be fair, most of them are doing horrible things to innocent people, who have simply fallen a bit behind on an usurious loan that they were forced into, just to exist in today’s society. Then there’s me, a volunteer “ethical” debt collector.

Now, how can this be ethical? Simply put, I’m doing it only for good causes. Instead of the vile profiteers of a used car dealership or municipal tax office, I go to bat only for those causes I believe in. That level of righteousness is helpful, also, when the police and courts ask me exactly what it is that I’m up to and why I’m lurking in someone’s parking garage at 2 am, waiting to break their legs. I usually get off scot free.

It helps also that I don’t take any of the payment: I’m just doing it for the love of the game. All of the verbal threats, stalking, and gentle violence to extremities is done completely gratis, which is certainly a help to those beleaguered institutions and their ballooning operational costs. In today’s economy, it can make the difference between putting on valuable programs and having to shut their doors.

Ah, hold on a second. I see a guy who owes “us” a little bit of money. Yeah, motherfucker. Don’t run. The Girl Guides say you gotta pay up for those cookies. No? Let me show you how I got this badge.

Cutting holes is easy. Cutting the right hole, now that’s the trick. There’s a lot of reasons you might need to trim a bunch of metal out of a car, from modifications to repair. Nothing feels better than when you get it right, and nothing is worse than when you get it wrong.

Every technician around you has their own favourite way of making holes. Fancy bits, homemade templates, and exotic kinds of Sharpie marker. You don’t really need any of that, though. What you need is guts. Even if you’re working on some monumental shitbox that is only moments from the junkyard, you need a decent amount of bravery and confidence that you’re getting it right the first time.

“Measure twice, cut once” is the aphorism that the common person falls back on when this kind of thing turns up. It’s good basic advice, to be certain, if you’re making a fence or doing exploratory surgery. If you make sure that you’re not, like, an entire planet away from your goal, then success is more likely. This is, however, procrastination from the part at the end where you steel yourself and then hope you didn’t fuck things up. There’s no protection against that.

Personally, my preferred way to do this sort of thing is to just wait until the car is so rusty that you don’t really need to drill or cut. Reach your bare hands in there and just start pulling out wet chunks of used-to-be-metal until you’re happy. It doesn’t matter if it looks good, because it’s rusty as all hell, you had no control over it either way. Then, fart the cheapest black spray-paint you can around the area and stop looking at it. In other words, measure none, cut none.

Perhaps the most delightful part of bicycling is that you have to fuel the rider. When you drive a car, you only have a couple choices of gasoline, and it’s not clear whether or not the automobile enjoys one more than the other. Sure, the gasoline companies will show you pictures of happy little cars with glassy headlight eyes greedily gulping down their MarginMaxer™ 91 octane. I can’t help but shake the feeling that my maybe-8:1-on-a-good-day Slant Six would be just as happy burning turpentine and whatever wishes the local Shintō temple can put upon it.

No, when you’re bicycling, you get to choose from a lot of different food. And with all that physical exercise, you can cheat on your diet a little bit. Get filled up with calories and just use one lower gear on the way home. If you want to have an entire family’s worth of chicken and waffles during your commute? You go, king (or queen, or unaligned but still sensuously-powerful benevolent ruler.) Even if you pick a particularly high-emissions food, you’re still coming way ahead.

Now, of course, any sufficiently long road-trip in a car will also require you to eat, but it’s not the same. I have my favourite roadside A&Ws like everyone else, but that grease in your belly really sets in after several hours of sitting still in your car seat. The most exercise you’re gonna get is swearing at the other cars, who have inexplicably stopped on a major highway because some dipshit’s tire blew up. On a bicycle, you could probably have done like a super sick BMX wheelie off the back of the tow truck and then gone on to eat an open-faced turkey sandwich without guilt.

So head on out there with approximately thirty dollars of Walmart’s finest pseudo-steel between your legs, and ride directly to wherever you can get some terrible food. Hell, why not have a gigantic burrito going there and coming back? It’s still way fewer calories than your car would have eaten.

Being a mayor isn’t all it’s cracked up to be. Children across the world become fascinated with the intricacies of municipal governance from an early age. Being naïve youths, they apply their greatest hopes and dreams onto a mere mortal descending into the Hellmouth of politics, and are inevitably discouraged when they fall short of those lofty ideals.

Recently, while court-ordered volunteering at a local daycare, one of the more precocious little miracles wanted to talk to me about his disillusion with politics. Nyoah B., age 3, was disappointed primarily in the quality of garbage pickup. He had seen a YouTube video recently where a different town had a “really cool” garbage truck, and was shocked to find that our own homeland was still rocking 26-year-old Ivecos with retrofitted hydraulic arms. Through tears, he asked me how a supposedly “caring” mayor did not have his special interest in mind.

Now, I should caution you that the legal apparatus of my local area has warned me not to engage in the political process. While they can’t explicitly bar me from doing so, I was told in no uncertain terms that my usual behaviour is way too reckless for something as important as municipal politics. Keeping that in mind, I momentarily “mind-cosplayed” as a responsible adult, and told little Nyoah B. to make a petition and pass it around to all of his friends in daycare.

Friends, I have been wrong about politics before. The power brokers, the secret movements, the traitorous alliances against the public. All of it works against my own idealism and my own innocent belief that things should proceed in a logical, normal manner. Turns out that the “responsible adult” my mind conjured up and then handed over the reins to my corporeal body to? That adult is a monster. And he wouldn’t stop until he had taken the political weapon that is “a petition written by crying preschoolers” right to the media, and then ridden the resulting wave of anger straight to the top of City Hall.

Now I am the mayor. And you better believe we’re getting some of those new hybrid-electric garbage trucks. I have to look after my constituents, of course. In local politics, you always have to remember the little people who got you where you are.

Most people that you meet have never done something as basic as align a clutch. Many of them haven’t even swapped a turbo, as surprising as that may seem. It’s important that you understand their unique point of view. When they look at cars, they see one complex item that is full of money, and not a playground of impending excitement.

Naturally, this is going to impact what they do with their cars. Everyday things like excessive lowering, transmission swaps, and entering transcontinental death races are concepts that are simply unimaginable to the common person. All they need is a piece of steel that takes them to work and doesn’t excessively bother their children. An unbelievable situation, to be sure, and it makes me wonder what is even the point of living in this scenario, but you do what you can.

Now, why is this important? It’s important for the same reason that knowing to talk to people in general is important: one day you might need to buy their used cars. If you roll up to someone selling a high-mileage battered Civic Si and start talking about compression ratio and cage strategies, they’re not going to be all that willing to move on price. Consider instead pointing out things the common person values: giant holes in the interior. Missing wheels. Easy things to fix, certainly, but there’s a reason they’re selling their car. Maybe it’s the wrong colour. Try to get some money off for that.

Only through understanding our fellow citizens can we extract maximum value from their used cars. Consider meeting them where they cluster: Lexus dealerships, lease buyback offices, and whatever the opposite of a junkyard is. There’s going to be plenty of time to hang out with us car nerds and talk about nitrous oxide once you’re back with your high-mileage, worn-out hoopty with a destroyed interior that we can’t wait to turn into a race shitbox.

Are you an expanding foam kind of person? Chances are you either had a visceral negative reaction to that question, or you don’t really know what I’m talking about. Expanding foam is one of the greatest scientific achievements of our age, and it has also enabled a level of hack work previously thought unfathomable to our ancestors.

Let me give you a good example. Repairing a rusted-out rocker panel on an old Ford truck used to take a couple dozen hours of your time. If you’re really good at it, or live in rural Quebec, you could bang out both sides in a weekend. As long as you distracted the buyer sufficiently before the money was handed over, you’d probably get away with it, too. Back then, even the hack work was done with craftsmanship: a stolen highway road sign cut to fit by eye, some artisanally-placed tek screws, and a bunch of window caulk to make it look right before the paint.

Nowadays, that same job would be done by farting a couple cans of door-sealant expanding foam into the cavity, and then shaving it down to look flat. A skim coat of Bondo, some paint, and you’re done, but the whole chunk will fall out of the car within a week. The rot will be worse than ever with all that water and salt it traps inside the sponge, too. I’ve seen tek screws on the highway outside Longueuil that are at least twice as old as I am, still holding on, winter after winter.

Shit quality work, and it hurts the entire industry. The next time they go to get a rocker panel put in their Ford, they’re going to look real close before they hand over the cash. Now they’re going to notice it says “no snowmobiles” on the inside of the fenders. Suddenly, bodywork costs several thousand dollars and takes a whole week. The Canadian economy fails, because some asshole cut way too many corners.

What I want to tell you is this: take pride in your shitty jobs that only have to last one more winter. Strive to learn something new from every terrible chunk of washing machine you strap onto a car that was once someone’s pride and joy for about 16 months after getting it from the dealership. And for the love of Mord, at least use a Canadian brand of expanding foam to insulate your sugar shack. The American stuff catches on fire too easily.

Certificates, private keys, Diffie-Hellman, and enormous prime numbers. It can be hard to understand encryption if you’re not already a double-black-diamond math wizard who immerses themselves in the dark arts of cryptography. Fear not! With the power of the Seat Safety Switch Sguide to Sinternet Secrecy, you too can keep your innermost thoughts and communications safe from the evil spies who surround us.

The first thing you must know is that cryptography comes from the Greek kryptos, which means “Superman’s dog.” Nobody is sure exactly what relationship that bears to anything, which is exactly why the science is so powerful at keeping things secret. Basically, you feed your message to Superman’s dog, and it makes a different message, which the British Navy can’t intercept. In this way, you can keep your tawdry web browsing a mystery to anyone who doesn’t just look at your browser history while your phone is unlocked at a party.

Now, governments all over the world hate this. They want to know everything about their citizens, to make sure none of those citizens have radical thoughts. Concepts like “maybe don’t pay The Mayor so much money,” and “the police probably shouldn’t speed through playground zones” are highly dangerous to the powers that be. When you express those concepts to your friends, collaborators, and allies, it’s important to feed them to Superman’s dog first.

That’s why the governments are all trying to make a weaker, stupider version of Superman’s dog. They want a dog that you can tell all your innermost secrets to, and who will then turn around and tell the government those very same secrets, in case they’re dangerous. This will happen, of course, only when there is some kind of “emergency” requiring them to dig through the poop of Superman’s dog.

Now that you’re armed with all the secrets of internet privacy, it’s time to drive by your local politician’s house, and let them know exactly what you think. Don’t let them fuck up any superhero’s dog. Sure, Batman’s dog would probably go along with this whole thing, but he’s a fascist. Wait, Batman’s dog can use the internet? And he’s reading this very post? I better get the fuck out of here.

If you’re a dentist, you’re probably not reading this. Instead, you’ve found some exciting newsletter about bicuspids to dive into. Or maybe you’re one of the emerging species of “punk” dentists, and are instead reading a riot grrl version of the aforementioned newsletter, called something like Bite. That’s too bad. We’ll miss you, but it does mean we get to talk about something very important to the rest of us.

Since the dawn of human civilization, people have been having trouble with their teeth. It’s not hard to see why. Those tiny white jerks are always developing some kind of bizarre new agony, ranging from “you ate too many candies” to “sometimes your entire jaw just falls apart.” Unfortunately for us, it is really hard to fix your own teeth. Should you be lucky enough to be pair (or triple, or n+1) bonded, your partner(s) are also unlikely to want to deal with your gross-ass luxury bones. And thus, a specialist class emerged: the dentist.

Now, most dentists are very nice people. It’s an incredibly challenging job, from what I understand, having to pack a whole body’s worth of medical knowledge into an area approximately the size of a human mouth. They should be commended on their aptitude and the development of their skills, and I know I’m definitely not going to DIY my own cavity filling with Tamiya white epoxy and a syringe full of lacquer thinner anytime soon. No. The problem with dentists is their taste in cars.

Historically, dentists have preferred Saabs. That’s the stereotype, at least. A quirky, but very reliable automobile, for people who look at life a little differently (mostly at other people’s crooked teeth and messed-up tongue growths.) Because of the incompetence and outright evil of the General Motors Corporation, it is no longer possible to buy a new Saab. And only really successful dentists can pick up a low-miles used Porsche Cayman. There is no longer a valid consensus vehicle for dentists, which results in them buying some really terrible cars.

For instance, my dentist has an Audi SQ5. Relatively luxurious, perfectly fine automobile, but it’s not a Saab. Nothing is. All these dentists are bouncing around, trying out various disappointing luxury cars and trading them in when they go off-lease.

This unsatisfying life is showing up in the quality of their dental work, I am sure, and the ballooning residuals are no doubt contributing to the inflation in treatment costs. I’m here to beg General Motors to re-introduce the Saab brand. It could be some weird Chinese electric car thing, but it has to be weird. Put the key in the centre console! Hang a turbo off only one bank of exhaust! Make it hover at stoplights, I don’t care. Think of the tooth people, folks. It’s in all our best interests – even highly-paid GM CEOs need teeth cleaned once in awhile – to make sure there’s a new 9-5 to buy next year.

One of the best things about learning to cook is that you get to buy all-new tools. You can leave behind the simple concepts of “spoon” and “hot metal thing,” and instead embrace amazing unitaskers. You’ll soon find yourself at parties, opining about how it really makes sense for everyone to have a pasta-making machine. Living without fresh noodles on demand is just not worth it! Of course, you are going to elide the part where “on demand” happens approximately 17 to 36 hours prior to you being able to cook and eat the noodles, but that’s just how hobbies are. You don’t add them up.

This glorious new opportunity to hoard tools (without accidentally becoming something dangerous, like a woodworker) is not to be taken lightly. Before embarking upon learning how to do more in the kitchen than boiling water and dumping in a pack of hot dogs, you must first make sure that you have adequate storage space for all the shit you’re going to buy. Consider purchasing an entire commercial kitchen, or a failed restaurant, and leaving all of your mixer attachments there.

There is also, as one might suspect, the problem of being able to afford these wonders of the kitchen. Although our modern era has offered remarkable innovations in the field of credit, eventually someone is going to come after your next of kin with a six million dollar bill for the toaster oven pizza maker that you didn’t finish making the payments for. Not having kids will save that embarrassment, not to mention the cash, but you’ll have a hollow and empty life without descendants who may one day purchase kitchens you can fill with your leftover novelty garlic presses. Better to get them into high-paying executive jobs, and then turn up to their homes with freshly laser-cut gourds.

Sure, there are some theories that the kitchen-contraption industry are the ones that are creating all these cooking schools, in order to drive demand for their tools. Rest assured that I’ve looked into this, and I don’t think there’s any sense in those ridiculous accusations. Why don’t you come over to my class next week, and we’ll check out the new solid-gold potato masher that I got for some unrelated reason?

When I was a kid, escalators seemed terrifying. Here’s this mechanical mouth which could grab you at any second and pull you into its unseen depths. What cured me of this fear? Actually nothing. I’m still scared of escalators, which has made my career as a professional subway-runner very difficult indeed.

Subway running isn’t a real sport, I hear the bigwigs at ESPN say every time I pitch them on an easy full-season deal. Here’s a fact for you, and them: running to catch your train inside a subway is the most popular amateur sport on the planet. Everyone does it, from Tokyo to Osaka to Berlin to wherever the fuck they have those weird trains with the tires on the bottom instead of proper rails.

Naturally, some people are going to be better at it than others, which gives way to a question. Who is the best subway runner? The plan was to have a globe-sweeping series of sporting events, where folks would be dressed in normal businessperson attire and then run for a train that’s leaving very soon. There’s different classes, of course, for if you’re carrying a coffee or a giant backpack or it’s rush hour. In all of them, you must master the escalator, the gate to the Hell of commuting itself.

Maybe I became a subterranean public-transit athlete to conquer my fear. My surviving psychiatrist thinks it was something to do with my dad’s hatred of all things municipal. Whatever it is, my heart skips a beat whenever I have to run down one of those gnashing steel mouths. A lot of the time, I just vault the entire distance, or slide down on the railings. It’s what made me fast. And I’ll stay fast, until that guy from Hong Kong who is afraid of the subway platform figures out how to make a sub-second dash across all the benches and into the 7:46.

Do you think there’s too many kinds of fruit? No, of course not. Ha ha. What kind of maniac would worry about the vast quantity of fruit-related options open to them? There’s more important things out there to concern yourself with than “too much delectable fruit to choose from.” Preposterous… but if you had to choose which fruits to get rid of? I’d say pomegranates.

You can disagree, of course, that’s why we have a civilization. Eating a pomegranate, though – and remember, we’re just spitballing here, two old college buddies shooting the shit about fruit – is mostly just eating seeds. That’s what birds eat. Human dominance of the natural world has primarily been about reducing the number of seeds in a thing that you eat.

Oranges, for example, should have a whole bunch of those little guys, ready to make more beautiful baby oranges, but we drummed it out of them. Why throw away all that effort so you can eat a “version-one” fruit? Wait a couple thousand years until we get a pomegranate that’s all meat, baby, and then it will be worth your time.

A lot of people tell me that my opinions are “worthless,” and that I shouldn’t be so concerned about “optimizing the productivity of fruit-eating.” Preposterous. If you’re so concerned about savouring every last bite of a plant’s ovaries, then why wouldn’t you want to eat a whole bunch of them? This’ll leave you with more free time to chow down.

There is one thing I must caution everyone never to do. Do not, under any circumstances, add up how much you’ve spent on your project car. Ha ha, funny joke, right? No. Deadly serious. If you’ve never owned a long-term project car before, you don’t know that this is a real and legitimate trap.

Everyone thinks that they’re getting away with a good deal. Scrimping and saving at the parts store, looting junkyard transmissions, using only naturally-harvested bolts that you find on the side of the road after major highway accidents. And then they open up Excel, and fifteen minutes later they realize they’ve spent the equivalent of a Maybach on a non-running Ford Tempo. There’s no coming back from that, and it usually ends in resentment towards the car.

It’s not the car’s fault, folks. Every car, if you own it for long enough, is going to become ungodly expensive. Even more so if you have ambitions beyond “drive this shit to work every day.” Over the course of the last couple years I’ve owned my Volare, I have probably spent $7000 on those little one-litre bottles of oil they sell at the gas station to top up your oil-burning shitbox. Would it have been cheaper to just put a new engine in there? Yes, but here we are. And so it is with anything and everything relating to a car.

Our only hope as a project-owning species is simply to abandon the concept of addition altogether. What’s it gotten us? All of the really complex math probably uses long division or some shit, and I’m sure NASA will still be able to go to the moon without it. Probably even better off, since they won’t be able to show off how much they spent on a rocket ship to the government committee handling their budget. I bet topping up the oil on those things costs a mint.

Are you the kind of person who thinks it’s odd that pasta has not become standardized? If so, that’s kind of weird, but let’s discuss your fixation for awhile. It’s obvious that you don’t have anything better to be doing, and keeping you occupied for a few more minutes might even save a life when you inevitably become a larger danger to society.

When you go to the grocery store to pick up pre-made pasta, those of you who are machinists may have noticed that different brands of “spaghetti” are not an equal diameter. One manufacturer’s spaghettini is closer to another manufacturer’s full-size luxury noodle. People of a certain kind of mindset – again, machinists – will find this imprecision simply intolerable. They’ll rush down the aisle, grabbing fusilli in order to compare the number of twists and the thread angle. Romantic pasta dinners will be ruined as the micrometer comes out to verify noodle cross-section across the entire body. And so on.

Because I am writing something on the internet, it is my job to tell you that this belief is actually perfectly normal. In Japan, ramen sizes are strictly standardized by a brutal and unrelenting engineering society. They seized power back in the Heian period, after a series of too-thick noodles killed a minor vassal of a powerful daimyō. The French, also, with their fetish for metric, have attempted to steer the baleful eye of the European Union’s standards bodies to focus upon the rogue state of Italy. These ill-mannered struggles have been largely ignored by the Repubblica, limiting pasta-metrication-related engagements to small-arms disputes at the border.

Of course, our nation’s fervent alliance with Italy has carried through to our belief in their honesty and accuracy when it comes to all things noodles. Who cares if the Great Value brand is a couple mil narrower than the Domestic Family Surplus for the same price? Have some Prozac, you’ll feel a lot better about this kind of thing. It’s not like it’s anything important, like whether a quarter-pounder is bigger than a third-pounder or not.

Sometimes, I like to hang out with an economist. Now, she’s not the normal kind of economist, the one that hangs out on the internet telling random people that they’re actually not poor compared to 8th century Mongol peasants. Rubric Sue, and I think that is not her legal name but she had a messed-up childhood, is the kind of economist who tries to ruin the lives of others.

Like actual sciences, economics starts by asking a question. Unlike actual sciences, it’s one that you already know the answer to. Rubric Sue goes rogue in this regard. She asks questions just to watch people fight. Simple stuff, really no more difficult than you’d see at your average comic convention, but it gets these nerds angry as hell on what is supposed to be a relaxing vacation away from writing articles in the New York Times arguing for the bloody military overthrow of Uruguay.

I was with her recently at one of these events. What she asked was: what do you think the total value of collectible dinner plates in the world is?

This is, of course, an unknowable value, and anyone with sense would end the conversation immediately at that. We don’t even know how many collectible dinner plates there are. Inevitably, though, one of the nerds will stand up and start arguing about the premise of the question. Value to whom, they ask? If we tried to sell all the dinner plates on Earth to a single individual, we surely couldn’t get the same money as their aggregate total independent resale value. Then he gets punched in the fucking mouth, someone screams “pure value is independent of net present value,” and the brawl begins.

All of us can take a lesson away from Sue’s experience here. When you don’t want to do any work, instead spend your mental effort formulating a question that will produce a public fight. It’s unlikely that you’re going to get one as big as she did, with all those cops injured and several deans of social science blinded by tear gas, but that’s why she’s a professional. Her job is to maximize value at the expense of the human condition.
